Lecture 17 · Random forests and boosting · Fri 27 Nov

- Bagging averages away a tree's variance; a random forest decorrelates the trees with `mtry`
- Boosting fits each small tree to the previous mistakes, slowly — the learning rate is the brake
- **Every tree in a forest is wrong; the forest is right because they are wrong in different ways**

## Objectives

- See where neural networks come from, and what problem they were built to solve
- Meet the **perceptron**, and train one by hand — four rows, two epochs, no software
- Understand gradient descent, the engine under every network
- Discover that a network with one neuron **is a GLM** — and what that buys you
- Add a hidden layer, and see flexibility and overfitting arrive together

## Why a manager cares

::: {.subtitle-frame}
The most over-sold and under-understood model in business, and in hospitals
:::

| | What the vendor sells | What you ask first |
|---|---|---|
| **Retailer** | "AI predicts which customers will leave" | does it beat a logistic regression on the same table? |
| **Hospital** | "AI reads the vitals and flags who will deteriorate" | does it beat the early-warning score the nurses already compute? |

: {tbl-colwidths="[16,42,42]"}

- Underneath the word *AI*, on a table of customers or patients, there is usually a neural network: a regression that learned to bend
- You will be asked to approve, fund, or trust one. Today: what it is. Friday: when it is the *wrong* tool, which on tabular data is most of the time

## [Section 1]{.section-kicker} From linear to nonlinear {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## The motivation, in one picture

{{< video media/Boundary.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

Invented ward patients: danger on every side of normal vitals. The best straight line, the kind logistic regression draws, misses 15; three hidden neurons, blended, miss 3.

## Two dialects, revisited

From lecture 10 — now it matters:

| Statistics | Machine learning |
|---|---|
| Coefficients | **Weights** $W$ |
| Intercept | **Bias** $W_0$ |
| Transformation, link | **Activation function** $g$ |
| Fitting | **Training** |
| Observations | **Training set** |

::: {.callout-important title="The trade, stated once more"}
You are about to gain flexibility and lose interpretability. A neural network learns *whatever* relationship is there. It does not tell you what it learned, and it gives you no standard errors. Choose it when prediction is the whole job.
:::

## [Section 2]{.section-kicker} The perceptron {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## McCulloch & Pitts, 1943

Inputs $X_1, \dots, X_p$, weights $W_1, \dots, W_p$, a bias $W_0$, and a step:

$$
\hat y \;=\; \operatorname{sign}\!\Big(W_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{p} W_j X_j\Big), \qquad \operatorname{sign}(z) = \begin{cases} +1 & z \ge 0 \\ -1 & z < 0\end{cases}
$$

In general: $\hat y = g\big[\phi(X; W)\big]$ — a **linear combination** $\phi$, then an **activation** $g$.

Now make both linear: $g(z) = z$. You have $\hat y = W_0 + \sum_j W_j X_j$. **That is linear regression.** The simplest possible neural network is the model you started the course with.

::: {.callout-note}
Inspired by the brain: *inputs* arrive like signals at dendrites, the *body* sums them, the *axon* fires or does not. The inspiration is real and the analogy is thin. Keep the picture; do not lean on it.
:::

## The difference that is not in the formula

Same equation, two philosophies:

- Linear regression has a **stochastic** part: $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$. The noise is in the model; that is where tests and intervals come from.
- The network is a **deterministic** map from input to output. No $\varepsilon$, no distribution, no inference — just *find weights that predict well*.
- Regression **imposes** the form of the relationship. The network **learns** it.

::: {.callout-note}
This is why a network can be more accurate and less useful at the same time. Both statements are about the same object.
:::

## Training: the perceptron rule

Supervised: we have the true $y$. Start with random weights, then for each observation:

$$
W(t+1) \;=\; W(t) + \eta\,(y - \hat y)\,X
$$

- $\eta \in (0, 1]$: the **learning rate** — how big a step. Set by you, not learned. A *hyperparameter*.
- $(y - \hat y)$: the error. Correct prediction → zero → no update.
- Wrong with $y = +1$: weights move *up* along $X$. Wrong with $y = -1$: *down*.

One pass over all observations is an **epoch**. Repeat until nothing changes, or you run out of patience.

## By hand: the AND gate

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Two binary inputs, output 1 only when both are 1. $W_1 = 0.3$, $W_2 = -0.1$, no bias, $\eta = 0.1$, threshold $\theta = 0.25$.
:::

| Obs | $X_1$ | $X_2$ | $y$ | $z$ | $\hat y$ | error | $W$ after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | — |
| 2 | 0 | 1 | 0 | −0.1 | 0 | 0 | — |
| 3 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0.3 | **1** | −1 | $(0.2,\,-0.1)$ |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0.1 | **0** | +1 | $(0.3,\,0.0)$ |

End of epoch 1: $W = (0.3, 0.0)$, two mistakes. Epoch 2: two more. Epoch 3: one. Epoch 4: none, $W = (0.2, 0.1)$, and it stops. Four rows, one rule, and the network has *learned* AND.

## By hand, watched

{{< video media/PerceptronByHand.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

The AND table, filled row by row: every product in epoch 1, then epochs 2–4 until one has no mistake. $W$ moves only on wrong rows, and only along that row's $X$.

## The same thing, as geometry

{{< video media/Perceptron.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

The shaded side is where it says 1, so a wrong row is a point on the wrong side. The line separates the gate in epoch 3; only epoch 4, with no mistake, proves it.

## [Drill 1]{.drill-kicker} Which alerts can one perceptron learn?

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · four alert rules for a medical ward
:::

| Rule | Inputs | Alert when |
|---|---|---|
| A | fever, heart rate over 100 (each 0 or 1) | both |
| B | fever, heart rate over 100 (each 0 or 1) | at least one |
| C | fever, heart rate over 100 (each 0 or 1) | exactly one: the two disagree |
| D | temperature, in °C | below 35.5 or above 38 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[10,50,40]"}

1. Sketch each rule: the four corners of the square for A–C, a line of temperatures for D. Which can a single perceptron learn?
2. The ward wants D, and a vendor offers a perceptron on temperature alone. What do you answer, and what one change makes it learnable?

## [Drill 1 · answer]{.drill-kicker} One perceptron, one straight line

- **A and B: yes.** A line cuts $(1, 1)$ off from the rest (A, the AND gate), or $(0, 0)$ off from the rest (B)
- **C: no.** No line puts $(0, 1)$, $(1, 0)$ on one side and $(0, 0)$, $(1, 1)$ on the other
- **D: no.** On one input a perceptron is one threshold, *above t* or *below t*; this alert has two ends
- **The fix for D**: two inputs, *below 35.5* and *above 38*. Then D is rule B, and B is learnable

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"One perceptron draws one straight line, and 'too cold or too hot' needs two cuts: give it the two flags as inputs, or a hidden layer that builds them."
:::

[Run in R from $W = (0.3, -0.1)$: A stops after 4 epochs, B after 5; C still makes 3 mistakes in epoch 100.]{.muted}

## [Section 3]{.section-kicker} Gradient descent {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## The general engine

The perceptron rule is a special case. Given a **loss** $L(W)$, say mean squared error, move the weights *downhill*:

$$
W_j(t+1) \;=\; W_j(t) - \eta\,\frac{\partial L(W)}{\partial W_j}
$$

- Derivative positive: decrease $W_j$; negative: increase it. The minus sign is the whole idea. Repeat until the gradient is near zero
- For a network, computing $\partial L / \partial W$ layer by layer is **backpropagation**: the chain rule, applied carefully

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
A network's loss is no bowl: you find *a* valley, which depends on the start. As with k-means, run it more than once.
:::

## The learning rate, and what it does to you

{{< video media/GradientDescent.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

From $W = 4$: $\eta = 0.3$ lands in 8 steps, $0.03$ is still short after 26, $1.05$ overshoots more at each step. Software shrinks $\eta$ as it goes (*annealing*) or adds *momentum*.

## Gradient descent on linear regression

Apply the update to $\hat y = XW$ with squared loss: $W(t+1) = W(t) + \eta\, X^\top(y - XW)$.

It converges to $\hat W = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y$. **Exactly OLS.** On 189 births (`MASS::birthwt`), birth weight in kg, predictors standardised, 100 steps of $\eta = 0.1$:

| | OLS, `lm()` | NN, identity activation |
|---|---|---|
| Intercept | 2.945 | $W_0$ = 2.945 |
| Mother's weight | 0.123 | $W_1$ = 0.123 |
| Mother's age | 0.038 | $W_2$ = 0.038 |
| Smoker | −0.132 | $W_3$ = −0.132 |

Identical coefficients, identical predictions. Nothing was gained — yet.

## [Section 4]{.section-kicker} One neuron is a GLM {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## The bridge

Train a network on the **negative log-likelihood** and gradient descent finds the **MLE**. More precisely: a single-neuron network with activation $g$ *is* a GLM whose link is $g^{-1}$.

| Target | Regression | Link $h(\mu)$ | Activation $g(\lambda)$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Continuous | Linear | identity | identity |
| Binary | Logistic | $\log \frac{\mu}{1-\mu}$ | sigmoid $\;\frac{1}{1+e^{-\lambda}}$ |
| Binary | Probit | $\Phi^{-1}(\mu)$ | $\Phi(\lambda)$ |
| Counts | Poisson | $\log \mu$ | $e^{\lambda}$ |
| Categorical | Multinomial | $\log \frac{\mu_k}{1-\mu_k}$ | softmax |

::: {.callout-note}
Invert the link and you have the activation, and back. You know every model in this table from Module 1.
:::

## The sigmoid, since it is everywhere

{{< video media/Sigmoid.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

On the step the slope is 0: gradient descent has no direction. The sigmoid's is $\sigma(1-\sigma)$, 0.25 at $\lambda = 0$. One sigmoid neuron with cross-entropy **is logistic regression**.

## [Section 5]{.section-kicker} Hidden layers {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Adding a layer

So far: input → output. Two layers, and nothing a GLM cannot do.

Now put $L$ **hidden neurons** between them. Each one is a little GLM of the inputs, and the output is a GLM of *them*:

$$
a_l = f\Big(W^{(1)}_{0l} + \sum_j W^{(1)}_{jl} X_j\Big), \qquad
\hat y = g\Big(W^{(2)}_0 + \sum_l W^{(2)}_l\, a_l\Big)
$$

- **Hidden**: you never observe $a_l$. They are features the network invents.
- Fully connected: every input feeds every hidden neuron. Weights: $(p+1)L + (L+1)$.
- Two activations, $f$ and $g$, and they are usually different.

## What a hidden layer buys

{{< video media/HiddenLayer.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

200 invented patients, at risk outside a safe BMI and blood-pressure oval. Each hidden neuron adds a line: 1, 2, 3, 4 neurons get 155, 174, 192, 197 of 200 right.

## Why the activations must bend

Set $f$ and $g$ both to the identity. Expand:

$$
\hat y = W^{(2)}_0 + \sum_l W^{(2)}_l \Big(W^{(1)}_{0l} + \sum_j W^{(1)}_{jl} X_j\Big) \;=\; \text{a linear function of } X
$$

- Three inputs, two hidden, one output: **11 weights** to express what **4** coefficients already did
- Same model, more parameters, less interpretability, nothing gained

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
A hidden layer with linear activations is over-parameterised linear regression. The bend comes from $f$ — sigmoid, tanh, ReLU. Without it, there is no network, only a slower way to run `lm()`.
:::

## More flexibility, and what it costs

{{< video media/Overfitting.mp4 width="880" height="495" >}}

40 hidden neurons, 161 weights, 50 training patients (6 labels flipped), 100 test. Test loss is lowest at iteration 85; at 385 training is perfect, test 32 of 100 wrong.

## Three ways to stop it

- **Early stopping**: watch a validation set; stop when its error turns up. Simple, empirical, no guarantee it is the true optimum
- **Regularisation**: add a penalty $\lambda J(W)$ to the loss. $J = \sum W^2$ is **ridge** — *weight decay* in the ML dialect. $J = \sum |W|$ is **lasso**. Same idea as Module 1, same $\lambda$ to tune
- **Fewer neurons**: the honest fix, and the one people resist

::: {.callout-note}
Everything from lecture 7 — ridge, lasso, cross-validation for $\lambda$ — applies unchanged. A network is a very flexible regression, and it overfits like one.
:::

## In R

```{.r code-line-numbers="1-2|4-5|7-8|10|12"}
library(tidyverse); library(nnet); library(ISLR2)
d <- Default |> mutate(default = default == "Yes", balance = scale(balance), income = scale(income))

set.seed(1); tr <- sample(nrow(d), 7000)

fit <- nnet(default ~ balance + income + student, data = d[tr, ],
            size = 5, decay = 0.01, maxit = 500, trace = FALSE)     # 5 hidden, weight decay

p <- predict(fit, d[-tr, ])                                          # probabilities

mean((p > 0.5) == d$default[-tr])                                    # held-out accuracy
```

`size` is $L$. `decay` is $\lambda$. Both are hyperparameters, and Friday's lab is about choosing them without lying to yourself.

## [Drill 2]{.drill-kicker} How many neurons for the diabetes clinic?

::: {.subtitle-frame}
In pairs · 10 minutes · `nnet` on `MASS::Pima.tr` (200 women) · errors on `Pima.te` (332 others)
:::

| Model | Weights | Training error | Test error |
|---|---|---|---|
| Logistic regression, `glm` | 8 | 22.5% | 19.9% |
| Network, 1 hidden neuron | 10 | 22.0% | 22.7% |
| Network, 2 hidden | 19 | 17.9% | 24.8% |
| Network, 5 hidden | 46 | 9.2% | 27.8% |
| Network, 20 hidden | 181 | 0.1% | 28.8% |

1. Which model fits the 200 training women best? Which predicts new women best?
2. A vendor shows you the 20-neuron network: "99.9% accurate". Your answer, in one sentence?
3. Which model goes into the clinic? Defend it in one sentence.

## [Drill 2 · answer]{.drill-kicker} More neurons, worse predictions

- **Training error** falls with every neuron, 22.5% → 0.1%: 181 weights for 200 women is enough to memorise them
- **Test error** rises, 22.7% → 28.8%, and the logistic regression beats every network: 19.9%
- **To the vendor**: 99.9% is measured on the women it learned from; on 332 it never saw, it misses 28.8%, more than a `glm`

::: {.callout-tip title="A sentence that defends it"}
"The logistic regression: it misclassifies fewer new patients than any network, 19.9% against 22.7% at best, and a clinician can read its eight coefficients as odds ratios."
:::

[Mean of ten seeds per row, `decay = 0`, `maxit = 2000`, inputs scaled with the training means. With `decay = 0.01` the best network reaches 20.6%: still behind.]{.muted}

## A neural network is a regression that learned to bend. Whether it needed to is the question you must answer before you fit one.  {.statement}
